name: Palmela
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct Cariban variety; Glottolog refs are wordlists only (Fonseca 1881, Nordenskiold 1915, Becker-Donner 1956); no phonology exists.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page palm1241 (references: da Fonseca 1881, Becker-Donner 1956, Nordenskiöld 1915; classification comments from Meira 2006, Howard 2001, Gildea 2012).
Wikipedia, 'Palmela language' (cites Kaufman 2007 in Asher & Moseley, Atlas of the World's Languages, 2nd ed.).
sources.note: Nothing on stress; reports second-hand that Kaufman (2007) considered Palmela 'phonologically divergent' from other Cariban languages and that by 1954 only Andre Paix remembered a few words.

sources.citation: Meira, Sérgio. 2006. A família lingüística Caribe (Karíb). Revista de Estudos e Pesquisas (FUNAI, Brasília) 3(1/2): 157-174.
sources.note: Nothing on Palmela phonology. States that Palmella (Rondônia) and Pimenteira (Piauí) are extinct Cariban languages known only from small explorers' vocabularies; classification table lists 'Palmella † (?)' tentatively in the Guianan branch. No stress statements at all in the article (no 'acento' anywhere).

sources.citation: Becker-Donner, Etta. 1956. Archäologische Funde am mittleren Guaporé (Brasilien). Archiv für Völkerkunde 11: 202-249. Palmela section pp. 237-244.
sources.note: Nothing. Reports that by her visit only the old Andre Paix remembered some 20 words; reprints Fonseca's vocabulary (pp. 240-244) beside a 20-word 'Vokabular Andre Paix' (p. 244; forms such as tarapóne, capitó, tapiú, wasä, tüupo). Only linguistic remark (p. 240): the sole notable lexical connections are with Galibi, so Palmela is counted as Cariban.

sources.citation: Nordenskiöld, Erland. 1915. Forskningar och äventyr i Sydamerika. Stockholm: Albert Bonniers förlag.
sources.note: Nothing. Palmela appears only on p. 327 (a few civilised Palmela at Las Piedras and Rio Mequens, 'som äro karaiber', with photo Bild 124) and p. 410; no wordlist, no linguistic remarks.

sources.citation: Fonseca, João Severiano da. 1881. Viagem ao redor do Brasil, 1875-1878. Vol. II. Rio de Janeiro: Typographia de Pinheiro & C. Palmela section pp. 190-201 (vocabulary pp. 193-196).
sources.note: Nothing about stress placement. The only pronunciation remark (pp. 190-191) concerns aspiration, v/u/gu/hu alternation and a soft r: 'A pronuncia é suave e quasi melodiosa, ligeiramente aspirada: assim óhno, olhos, e ohóna, nariz... O r é, como em quasi todos os dialectos americanos, sempre brando.' The ~150-word vocabulary carries Portuguese-style acute/circumflex accent marks (meréma, páno, kihé, húre, tokéne, morúpa, paputáre, tuna, cápe, óca...), which are implicit stress notations with no explanatory statement.

sources.citation: Gildea, Spike. 2012. Linguistic studies in the Cariban family. In L. Campbell & V. Grondona (eds.), The Indigenous Languages of South America, 441-494. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
